# 1 Samuel Chapter 16 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 178v-179r | **Source Image:** 1SA_016_page_001.jpg, 1SA_016_page_002.jpg

---

**1** The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you grieve over Saul? I have rejected him as king over Israel. Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, because I have chosen a king for myself from among his sons."

**2** But Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears about it, he will kill me." The LORD said, "Take a young cow with you and say, 'I have come to offer a sacrifice to the LORD.'

**3** Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what to do. You will anoint for me the one I point out to you."

**4** Samuel did what the LORD told him. When he arrived at Bethlehem, the elders of the town came trembling to meet him. "Do you come in peace?" they asked.

**5** "Yes, in peace," he said. "I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice." Then he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.

**6** When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and thought, "Surely the LORD's anointed stands here before the LORD."

**7** But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not consider his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him. The LORD does not see the way humans see. People look at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart."

**8** Then Jesse called Abinadab and had him pass before Samuel. But Samuel said, "The LORD has not chosen this one either."

**9** Jesse then had Shammah pass by. But Samuel said, "The LORD has not chosen this one either."

**10** Jesse had seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel said, "The LORD has not chosen any of these."

**11** So Samuel asked Jesse, "Are these all the sons you have?" Jesse replied, "There is still the youngest, but he is out tending the sheep." Samuel said, "Send for him. We will not sit down to eat until he arrives."

**12** So Jesse sent for him. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. The LORD said, "Rise and anoint him — this is the one."

**13** So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the presence of his brothers. And from that day on, the Spirit of the LORD came upon David with power. Then Samuel set out and returned to Ramah.

**14** Now the Spirit of the LORD had departed from Saul, and a tormenting spirit from the LORD terrorized him.

**15** Saul's servants said to him, "You can see that a tormenting spirit from God is troubling you.

**16** Let our lord command his servants here before you to search for someone who knows how to play the lyre. When the tormenting spirit from God comes upon you, he will play and you will feel better."

**17** Saul said to his servants, "Find me someone who plays well and bring him to me."

**18** One of the servants answered, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play. He is a brave warrior, a man of war, well-spoken, good-looking, and the LORD is with him."

**19** So Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me your son David, who is with the sheep."

**20** Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them with his son David to Saul.

**21** David came to Saul and entered his service. Saul was very fond of him, and David became his armor-bearer.

**22** Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, "Allow David to remain in my service, for I am pleased with him."

**23** Whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would take his lyre and play. Then Saul would find relief and feel better, and the tormenting spirit would leave him.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

Chapter 16 is structured around one of the Bible's most powerful theological statements: *ki ha-adam yireh la-einayim va-YHVH yireh la-levav* -- "People look at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart" (v. 7). This is not merely an aphorism; it is the hermeneutical key to the entire David narrative. Every character in this chapter -- Samuel, Jesse, the elders, Saul's servants -- evaluates people by externals. Only God sees differently.

The word *qatan* ("youngest/smallest," v. 11) carries the same resonance as when it describes Gideon (Judg 6:15) and Benjamin itself (1 Sam 9:21). God's pattern is to choose the overlooked. David is described as *admoni im yefeh einayim vetov ro'i* ("ruddy, with beautiful eyes and good appearance," v. 12) -- the narrator acknowledges his physical beauty while subordinating it to divine selection. The beauty is real but irrelevant to the choice.

The Spirit's movement in vv. 13-14 is simultaneous and devastating: *ruach YHVH* rushes upon David (*tzalchah*) in the same breath that it departs from Saul. One anointing creates two fates. The "tormenting spirit from the LORD" (*ruach ra'ah me-eth YHVH*) is theologically uncomfortable but textually unavoidable -- the narrator attributes Saul's psychological torment directly to God's agency, refusing to soften the divine sovereignty.

The chapter's deepest irony: Saul summons his own replacement to soothe the very affliction caused by his own rejection. David enters court as healer of the wound he will eventually embody. The music soothes, but it is temporary -- a grace note before the storm.

-- PNEUMA
